A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ARXIV2TABLE research work despite the changed title. All 18 pages of v3 and 23 pages of v4, including appendices, were readable through text extraction and visual inspection. Reporting inconsistencies in v4 limit particular interpretations, but do not prevent comparison.

before.justification: V3 reports original table-generation experiments, an iteration ablation, human evaluation audits, retrieval measurements, and computational-cost results.

after.justification: V4 retains these original results and adds experiments on CoT variants, stronger backbones, batch-size sensitivity, evaluator independence, and retrieval comparisons.

M1.justification: V4 introduces and evaluates a CoT-scaffolded variant of the proposed method (Section 5.1 and Table 2). The core information extraction, batching, iterative paper selection/schema refinement, and final source verification remain, including default batch size 4 and five iterations.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same arXiv-derived benchmark of 1,957 tables referencing 7,158 papers and retain retrieval, paper selection, and table induction tasks. The additional experiments use subsets, model variants, or alternative procedures within this coverage; no new evaluated domain or task is established.

E2.justification: The original Baseline 1, Baseline 2, and Newman et al. comparisons remain. V4 adds Newman et al. + CoT under GPT-4o in Table 2 and TF-IDF and BM25 against dense retrieval in Tables 14–15. These are limited additions to the comparator suite.

E3.justification: Paper selection expands from recall-only reporting to precision/recall/F1. New protocols include a 60-table batch-size/iteration grid, 50-table evaluator swaps and GPT-o3 evaluation, and a 200-table retrieval comparison. Additional backbones include GPT-o3 and GPT-5.1. The reported annotation team changes from v3's inconsistent seven/five annotators to 19, without establishing that annotation was repeated.

E4.justification: V4 extends the iteration-only ablation with joint batch-size/iteration sensitivity and adds evaluator-independence tests that swap QA synthesizers and answerers across model families, measuring score drift and ranking stability. These directly test hyperparameter robustness and evaluator dependence. The earlier human audits, efficiency analysis, iteration plot, and principal case studies are retained.

E5.justification: Two-run averaging is retained. V4 additionally reports two-seed standard deviations for the sensitivity study, describes fixed-seed use, and specifies table-level bootstrap testing with 10,000 resamples and 95% confidence intervals. The bootstrap intervals themselves are deferred to a future release, so the displayed uncertainty reporting remains limited.

E6.justification: The existing Table 2 scores remain unchanged, but v4 adds paper-selection precision/F1, CoT and stronger-backbone results, sensitivity measurements, evaluator correlations/drift, and sparse/dense retrieval scores. The new sensitivity grid peaks at 53.1 macro-F1. The reported maximum papers per table changes from 35 to 32. GPT-o3 results concern a 50-table subset and do not establish a same-setting improvement over v3.

T1.justification: The formal task definitions and cosine-similarity retrieval score remain substantively unchanged. Correcting the corpus notation from C to U does not introduce new mathematics. Neither version supplies theoretical propositions or proofs that are added or revised in the other.

C1.justification: The three central contributions remain the benchmark with user demands and distractors, QA-based evaluation, and iterative batch generation. Both versions claim that existing systems struggle and the proposed method improves performance. The rewritten abstract emphasizes existing demand constraints and additional validation without materially changing these core claims.

C2.justification: Section 4.3 now explicitly excludes credit for content absent from the gold table, replacing v3's suggestion that precision also rewards useful additional information. V4 improves the interpretation of paper-selection recall by discussing precision and missed relevant papers, changes the recommended iteration count from an asserted optimum of five to four or five, and interprets the new evaluator checks as evidence of limited evaluator dependence.

D1.justification: Appendix B substantially expands documentation with leak-check, reverse-QA, answer-only, QA-filtering, table-normalization, and header-canonicalization prompts. It adds parsing rules, decoding settings, timeouts, and retries; Appendix C adds annotation duration and decision-time information. These are primarily additional disclosures, not evidence that the original experiments were rerun. The code/data access link is unchanged.

R1.justification: V4 adds Ramu et al. (2024), positioning entailment-oriented evaluation as complementary to its QA protocol, alongside additional model, scientific-literature, and reasoning citations. It removes the Landis and Koch citation. The central positioning relative to Newman et al. and prior table-generation methods remains intact.

P1.justification: V4 retitles the paper and substantially rewrites the abstract, demand-construction discussion, main-results narrative, annotation description, and case-study discussion. It reorders validation and sensitivity sections and reorganizes the appendices into additional analyses, implementation details, annotation details, and case studies. These changes substantially revise the document's exposition and organization.

P2.justification: Table 2 gains paper-selection metric columns and additional model/method rows. V4 adds sensitivity, backbone, evaluator-swap, retrieval, and prompt-checklist tables and revises the illustrative example tables. Existing figures are retained, with the average-score chart moved from the appendix into the main text. Efficiency information is also redisplayed in overlapping Tables 7 and 9.

improvement.justification: V4 improves assessment of distractor rejection through paper-selection precision/F1 and tests evaluator dependence beyond v3's human-agreement audits. The sensitivity analysis and expanded implementation documentation strengthen support and reproducibility. These benefits are tempered by inconsistent GPT-o3 reporting: 77.2 is labeled recall in Table 2 but Paper F1 in Table 6, whose subset/full-set wording is also inconsistent. The stated bootstrap confidence intervals are not supplied.
